reason: The provided sources easily support a high-stakes 45-second story with 13 distinct multi-sourced claims.
story: In November 2014, after a ten-year journey through space, the European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from the Rosetta spacecraft to attempt humanity's first soft landing on a comet. However, as Philae reached Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko, both its downward thruster and anchoring harpoons failed to fire. Instead of latching onto the surface, the lander bounced off the comet, soaring nearly one kilometer back up into space. It bounced a second time before coming to a rest over two hours later, wedged sideways inside a dark cliff shadow. Unable to get enough sunlight to recharge its solar batteries, Philae worked tirelessly for about 64 hours, sending back historic scientific data and images before entering hibernation. Months later in June 2015, it briefly reawakened to transmit signals. Rosetta finally photographed the silent probe in September 2016, right before ending its own mission by descending onto the comet.
angle: When Philae attempted humanity's first comet landing, its harpoons failed, sending the probe bouncing a kilometer back into space before wedging sideways inside a dark cliff shadow.

claims.claim: Philae launched in March 2004 on a ten-year journey to comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko onboard the Rosetta spacecraft.
Philae achieved humanity's first-ever soft landing on a comet nucleus on 12 November 2014.
The lander's anchoring harpoons failed to deploy upon initial contact with the comet.
Philae's cold-gas thruster failed to fire to hold the probe down on the comet surface.
Because it failed to anchor, Philae bounced twice off the comet's surface, touching down three times total.
During its first rebound, Philae rose to an altitude of about 1 kilometer (0.6 miles) above the comet surface.
Philae came to a final rest canted on its side inside a dark cliff shadow or crevice.
Because it landed in shadow, Philae received insufficient sunlight to recharge its secondary batteries via its solar panels.
Philae transmitted scientific data for about 60 to 64 hours before running out of main battery power and hibernating.
Instruments on Philae detected complex organic compounds on the comet.
In June 2015, Philae reawakened and briefly re-established communication with Rosetta.
Rosetta located and photographed Philae wedged in a dark crevice in September 2016.
The Rosetta spacecraft concluded its mission on 30 September 2016 by descending onto comet 67P.

disputed: Initial statements by mission controllers reported that harpoons had successfully fired and rewound, which was quickly corrected when telemetry revealed harpoons had not fired; attribute initial reporting confusion or omit early erroneous statements.

Exact dimensions and nature of the final landing crevice vary across sources (a deep crack in a cliff shadow versus a 2-meter deep hole); script should describe it generally as a dark crevice or shadow.
